I've also been feeling really scattered during meetings and have been losing my patience with my family.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever have sudden episodes of intense fear or panic that peak within minutes, with symptoms like a racing heart, shortness of breath, chest pain, or feeling like you might lose control?\n\nPatient: No, I don't really experience those sudden, overwhelming spikes of panic or things like chest pain. It’s more of a constant, lingering worry and physical tension that just stays with me throughout the entire day.\n\nDoctor: How much is this constant worry affecting your daily life, such as your work performance, relationships, or ability to get things done?\n\nPatient: It’s having a major impact, to the point where I'm missing details in my lesson plans, procrastinating on grading, and my principal noticed I seem scattered in meetings. At home, I'm turning down friends, missing my son's games, and my wife is deeply worried that this constant stress is completely overshadowing our family time.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever have brief periods of feeling unusually energized or needing much less sleep than usual, with racing thoughts or impulsive behavior?\n\nPatient: No, I definitely don't have periods of high energy or needing less sleep like that. In fact, it's the exact opposite—I feel constantly drained, exhausted, and physically tense from all the non-stop worrying.\n\nDoctor: Is your worry mostly about many different areas of life at the same time, or is it mainly focused on school and work? Also, do you find it hard to control the worry even when you know it may be excessive?\n\nPatient: It definitely goes beyond school now—I find myself constantly worrying about our family finances and whether I'm being a good husband and dad, even though I know it's blown out of proportion. I also find it impossible to control, like an unstoppable background loop in my mind that just keeps running no matter how hard I try to distract myself or tell myself to stop.\n\nDoctor: How has your sleep been over the past several months—do you have trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up feeling unrested?\n\nPatient: Even when I get to bed at a reasonable hour, I still wake up feeling completely exhausted and unrested. I end up dragging myself through classes feeling like I’ve already taught a full day before the first period even starts. Even though I'm sleeping, I just don't feel refreshed at all.\n\nDoctor: Do you also have periods of sudden, intense anxiety that come on quickly and peak within minutes, with symptoms like a racing heart, shortness of breath, chest pain, or feeling like you might lose control?\n\nPatient: No, I don't get those sudden, intense panic attacks or things like a racing heart and chest pain. For me, it's more of a constant, steady background worry and physical tension that stays with me throughout the entire day rather than coming on in sudden bursts.\n\nDoctor: Have you started any new medications, caffeine/energy drink use, or had any medical problems like thyroid issues that could be contributing to the anxiety?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't started any new medications, and I don't have any medical issues like thyroid problems. I also haven't increased my caffeine or energy drink intake at all. When I say I feel like I've had too much coffee, it's really just that physical feeling of restlessness, not from actually drinking more of it.\n\nDoctor: Over the past several months, have you also been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?\n\nPatient: I've definitely lost the enjoyment in things I used to love, like my robotics club, community theater, baseball, and playing with my son. I feel too drained and keyed up by the constant worry to participate, so I usually just end up sitting on the couch. However, it feels more like being completely overwhelmed and run-down by the anxiety rather than feeling hopeless or clinically depressed.\n\nDoctor: Over the past several months, have you been feeling down, depressed, or hopeless most of the day nearly every day, or is it mainly the constant worry and tension that is bothering you?\n\nPatient: It is definitely the constant worry and physical tension that is the main problem. I don't feel hopeless or depressed, but I am just completely worn out because my mind is always racing and I can't find a way to turn it off.\n\nDoctor: Do you also experience any of these with the worry: muscle tension, feeling restless or on edge, fatigue, trouble concentrating, irritability, or sleep problems? If so, which ones are the most bothersome?\n\nPatient: Yes, I experience almost all of those, especially the overwhelming fatigue that leaves me completely wiped out, and feeling scattered and impatient at home. Physically, I feel incredibly restless—like I've had too much coffee—and the muscle tension in my neck and shoulders is so severe that I constantly get dull headaches and a clenched jaw. The constant physical tension and fatigue are definitely the most bothersome because they completely prevent me from relaxing and spending quality time with my family.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a traumatic event, and if so, do you have nightmares, flashbacks, or try to avoid reminders of it?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't experienced any major traumatic events, and I don't have nightmares or flashbacks. My struggle is really just this constant, daily stress and anxiety about my job and trying to manage all of my responsibilities.\n\nDoctor: Do you have any repetitive, unwanted thoughts or rituals—like checking, counting, or reassurance-seeking—that you feel driven to do to reduce your anxiety?\n\nPatient: No, I don't have any of those repetitive rituals, checking, or counting behaviors. My mind is just constantly running through my actual, real-life responsibilities, like lesson plans and emails, rather than those kinds of rituals.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any periods of feeling depressed, hopeless, or losing interest in things for at least two weeks, separate from the constant worry?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't had any separate periods of feeling depressed or hopeless. While I've been less involved in my hobbies like the robotics club and theater, it's not a separate issue; I'm just too physically exhausted and mentally consumed by the constant worry about school to participate in them.\n\nDoctor: Did your anxiety start after a specific stressful event or life change, and does the worry feel clearly tied to that situation? Or does it continue even when things are going well?\n\nPatient: It started about seven or eight months ago when my school district rolled out a major curriculum overhaul and a new evaluation system. While it began as work-related stress, the worry has taken on a life of its own and spilled into other areas, like our family finances and whether I'm being a good husband and dad. Now, I just can't seem to shut it off, even when I'm trying to relax or when things are going perfectly fine.\n\nDoctor: Did your anxiety and worry start within a few months of the school change, and has it been much more intense than you would expect from that stressor alone? Or has it clearly lasted beyond what you think that situation should cause?\n\nPatient: Yes, it started about seven months ago, almost immediately after the new curriculum and evaluation system were rolled out. The worry feels completely blown out of proportion and much more intense than it should be, as it has taken over my evenings and weekends and has me constantly imagining worst-case scenarios.\n\nDoctor: Since the school change started, have your symptoms been present for the entire time and clearly more intense than you would expect from that stress, or did they begin after a major life event and then gradually improve as you adjusted?\n\nPatient: Yes, they’ve been present the entire time—about seven months now since the changes started. They haven't improved or gotten easier to manage at all; instead, the worry has just steadily mounted and feels completely out of proportion to the actual situation.\n\nDoctor: Did your anxiety and worry start after the school changes and stay clearly tied to that stress, or has it continued even when the stressor was no longer present or was much less intense?\n\nPatient: It started with the school changes about seven months ago, but it has definitely expanded way beyond that initial stress. Now, the worry continues constantly even when I'm at home trying to relax, spilling over into things like our family finances and whether I'm being a good husband and dad. It has taken on a life of its own and doesn't seem tied to just the school pressure anymore.\n\nDoctor: Did your symptoms begin within a few months of the school changes and stay clearly tied to that stress, or have they continued even when the stress was much less intense or not present?"
